title: Streaming chat: soft-retries + event-level telemetry cookbook
creator: Ava Park
description:
Problem: Customers building conversational experiences see two common failure modes with streaming chat: (1) transient network/transport errors cause the stream to drop mid-response and naive client retries either produce duplicated tokens or force the server to regenerate long context; (2) observability is coarse — it's hard to correlate partial event frames to latency/cost and identify where retries contributed to extra tokens.

Goal: Define a pragmatic, developer-friendly pattern for "soft retries" at the event level combined with event-to-trace telemetry so SDKs can resume streams with minimal duplication and operators can reason about retry behavior and unit economics. Produce a cookbook for the Python SDK (API surface, example code, and tests) and a short compatibility guideline for TypeScript/Go SDKs.

Proposal summary:
- Introduce an optional soft-retry contract on streaming responses: each event frame includes a stable event_id and a checkpoint cursor (cursor is an opaque string from the server representing the last committed state).
- Client-side behavior: on transient failure, attempt a resume call that supplies the last-seen event_id and cursor. The server returns a continuation stream starting from the next logical event. If the server cannot resume (cursor expired or model variant changed), it returns a resume-failure frame and the SDK falls back to a full re-request with an idempotency key.
- Idempotency + deduplication: SDK maintains an ordered buffer of emitted tokens/events and uses event_ids to dedupe any overlapping frames if resume returns overlapping content. Soft-retry favors emitting already-seen tokens only if the resume-start event_id is strictly greater than the last-acked id.
- Backpressure-aware resume: when resuming, the SDK recalculates the consumer window (max buffered tokens) to avoid unbounded memory growth. Resume attempts are rate limited by an exponential backoff with jitter (configurable policy).
- Telemetry mapping: each event frame is mapped to a trace/span with attributes: event_id, cursor, bytes_sent, bytes_recv, model_variant, resume_attempt (int), and cost_estimate_tokens. Resume attempts create child spans and a top-level retry_count attribute. These are surfaced to the Console as tagged metrics and per-request timelines.

API ergonomics (Python):
- Stream object prototype (high level):
  - chat = client.chat.stream(...)
  - for evt in chat:  # evt has .type, .event_id, .cursor, .text, .role, .delta
      process(evt)
  - chat.resume_if_transient(last_event_id=chat.last_event_id)
  - chat.on_resume(handler)  # optional hook for app-level metrics or token attribution

Developer ergonomics rationale:
- Keep the iterator shape for ease of use in existing code.
- Provide explicit resume API to avoid hidden retries that surprise developers and complicate billing.
- Expose event-level telemetry hooks so apps can attribute cost and latency to partial frames and retries.

Compatibility and fallback rules:
- If the server does not support resume, the resume API returns ResumeNotSupported error; SDK falls back to a full request using the same idempotency key.
- If resume fails due to expired cursor, SDK surfaces a RetryRequired error to the app with guidance to re-ask the user or perform a full regen.

Testing and acceptance criteria:
- Unit tests: simulate interleaved event sequences with overlapping tokens on resume and assert dedupe correctness.
- Integration: end-to-end test against staging server that simulates TCP drops and ensures resume succeeds within 2 attempts 95% of the time for default cursor TTL.
- Telemetry: Grafana panel shows resume_count per 1k streams and token-duplication metric under 0.1% for normal traffic.

Deliverables:
- Python SDK changes: resume API, event metadata parsing, dedupe buffer, telemetry hooks, and tests.
- Design doc (Confluence) + example notebook showing common server-side fallback patterns.
- Short TS/Go shim spec for parity.
